fixes.find: Yes, and most commercial duct work is staged that way. Sealing and damper work happens zone by zone, and ceiling tiles go back the same day. Noisy cutting gets grouped into after-hours or weekend blocks. Phasing costs a little more labor and avoids closing a floor.
fixes.replace: Often, depending on access and the scope in the written proposal. Sealing and damper work can usually be done zone by zone, and whether ceiling tiles go back the same day depends on the area opened and the building rules. fixes.find: As a general rule, mechanical alteration work in Chicago is permitted work, and scale decides the path. A like-for-like duct repair is not the same filing as a new layout tied to a build-out. Larger alteration work is recorded against a City of Chicago permit. Occupied buildings carry a second obligation. Where the landlord supplies heat, the Chicago Heat Ordinance (Municipal Code 13-196-410) sets a floor. It is at least 68 degrees from 8:30 a.m. to 10:30 p.m., and 66 degrees overnight, from September 15 to June 1.
fixes.replace: Often, and scale decides the path. Many mechanical alterations in Chicago need a City of Chicago permit, and a like-for-like duct repair may be treated differently from a new layout tied to a build-out, so confirm the requirement for the specific scope with the City before work is scheduled. Mixed-use buildings can carry a second obligation. Where the landlord supplies heat to apartments, the Chicago Heat Ordinance (Municipal Code 13-196-410) sets minimums for those dwelling units: at least 68 degrees from 8:30 a.m. to 10:30 p.m. and 66 degrees overnight, from September 15 to June 1. Heat in commercial-only space is usually a matter for the lease.
fixes.why: MAJOR 4: Heat Ordinance scoped to dwelling units in mixed-use buildings; permit claim made conditional
